transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-05 15:00 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Ruth Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Quasar CTO), Jon Kim (Lead ML Eng), Priya Singh (Infra)

Summary: quick technical deep dive focused on p95/p99 tail latency causes and mitigations. Covered KV cache hit patterns, batching tradeoffs, quantization impact on latency/throughput, and networking (VPC / on-prem hops + egress). Agreed to run benchmarks with streaming and non-streaming modes and produce a detailed tail-latency report.

Topics: p95 vs p99 behaviors, streaming vs non-streaming, continuous batching, KV cache warmup, quantization (int8/4bit) latency overhead, network hops impact (LB, NAT, firewall), VPC peering and performance, dedicated capacity vs hosted.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samir, AE on the account. We'll let Ruth take through the deep dive - Ruth are you on?
[00:07] Ruth Chen: Yeah hi, hi. Ruth here, SE. Thanks for the context Maya. Uh quick note, sorry if audio is a little crunchy on my end.
[00:12] Maya Lopez: No problem. We appreciate you doing this. We've been seeing some pretty bad tail latency on a couple of our endpoints, p99 spikes that knock our UX threads out.
[00:20] Jon Kim: To add, it's mainly the chat completion flow with streaming turned on for some endpoints, and another non-streaming bulk generate for enterprise reports. Both show odd p99s.
[00:28] Priya Singh: From infra side, we have a VPC peered to your hosted service over a transit gateway. There's a firewall and NAT in the path plus an internal load balancer.
[00:36] Ruth Chen: Great, that's exactly the variables we want to tease apart - infra hops + streaming vs non-streaming + model runtime. I'll share a quick mental model first.
[00:43] Ruth Chen: So p95 reflects common latency, p99 shows the extreme tail - often caused by factors like cold KV cache, re-loading weights, GC pauses, network retries, or batching misalignment. With streaming you'll see per-chunk latency metrics as well which can compound.
[01:01] Jon Kim: Can you clarify batching misalignment?
[01:03] Ruth Chen: Sure - if requests arrive at irregular rates, our continuous batching tries to wait a short micro-batch window to group tokens. If a request misses the batch window it can either be delayed for the next batch or be served alone resulting in a high per-token latency. That effect shows up more at p99.
[01:18] Samir Patel: We often see customers trade latency vs throughput by tuning the batch window (milliseconds). For low-latency UX flows we recommend smaller batch windows or enabling prefix KV cache to avoid recompute.
[01:30] Maya Lopez: We're using KV cache heavily - our multi-turn chat re-uses prefixes. But our observation is that p99 only improves after about 20k requests, i.e., when cache warms. Is that expected?
[01:40] Ruth Chen: Yeah some of that's workload shape - if the cache key cardinality is large you get lower hit rates. Also cache eviction and shard locality matter. Can you share hit rate numbers?
[01:50] Jon Kim: Our analytics show ~45% KV hit rate overall, but it's much higher for a subset of users. We do per-user prefixes so lots of cold keys.
[01:58] Ruth Chen: So that's consistent: cold keys will cause model to compute from scratch which increases both median and tail. For p99 spikes you often want to instrument per-key latency and maybe pre-warm heavy users if feasible.
[02:10] Priya Singh: From networking, NAT timeouts and occasional re-resolution to another AZ have caused about 50-200ms extra hops on some requests. That could be showing up in p99.
[02:20] Ruth Chen: Absolutely - networking jitter adds to the tail. We usually recommend either Dedicated (to reduce cross-tenant routing) or Private deployment with VPC peering to remove extra public hops.
[02:30] Maya Lopez: Can you say more about Dedicated vs Private? Our security team prefers VPC or on-prem for compliance, but cost is a concern.
[02:37] Samir Patel: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools in Redwood cloud - less noisy neighbor, predictable throughput, but still a managed control plane. Private (VPC or on-prem) gives you full network control and removes external egress points, which can shave off the network-induced tail. Pricing differs as expected. We'll include a breakdown.
[02:52] Jon Kim: Ruth, about streaming vs non-streaming - we saw that enabling streaming sometimes increases p99 because the server flushes chunks; other times it's lower because user sees early tokens. How do we reason about that?
[03:03] Ruth Chen: Good question. Streaming reduces time-to-first-byte by returning partial tokens quickly, improving perceived latency. But if your app waits for end-of-stream or aggregates chunks, the backpressure and chunk flush timing can increase tail variance. Also, streaming requires more frequent network packets - so opportunities for network jitter increase.
[03:20] Maya Lopez: That tracks. Our chat UI renders as tokens arrive, but for audit logs we aggregate, so the bulk path becomes non-streaming and shows worse p99.
[03:28] Ruth Chen: For those, consider dual-path: stream to UI, but write end-of-generation outputs asynchronously to audit store. Also, configuring smaller streaming chunk sizes can reduce p99 in some topologies.
[03:38] Jon Kim: Let's talk quantization: we're exploring int8 and 4-bit quant. Does that change tail behavior?
[03:44] Ruth Chen: Quantization usually reduces per-token compute latency and memory bandwidth, improving throughput and median latency. However, quantized kernels can introduce different kernel selection paths and occasional fallback to slower kernels for certain sequence lengths, which can cause p99 spikes if your runtime picks a non-optimal kernel at high seq lengths.
[04:02] Samir Patel: We saw one customer where 4-bit gave 30% lower median, but p99 remained because of IO stalls on KV cache retrieval. So it's important to benchmark full stack: network + runtime + cache, not just model op latency.
[04:15] Priya Singh: On the subject of KV cache, would sharding cache across GPUs help tail? We have multi-GPU Dedicated in mind.
[04:21] Ruth Chen: Yes, locality helps. If the KV cache lives in the same GPU host where the request is served, you avoid host-to-host transfers. Our runtime uses local device KV when pinned to a worker. But cross-host cache fetches can add 1-5ms per hop, ballooning for p99 in bursty scenarios.
[04:36] Maya Lopez: Is there instrumentation we can run? We want per-hop latency, kernel selection logs, and cache hit traces.
[04:42] Ruth Chen: We can enable tracing - Redwood traces include: request ingress time, LB egress/ingress, KV cache lookup time (per-key), kernel execution time, and post-process tokenization. We'll add those to the benchmark.
[04:53] Jon Kim: We'll need to obfuscate PII before sending traces to you.
[04:56] Samir Patel: Totally - we support redaction and you can share sanitized traces.
[05:00] Ruth Chen: Walkthrough of proposed benchmark plan: 1) Run synthetic replay of Quasar production trace (drop-in sample) across three modes: streaming small-chunks, non-streaming, and hybrid; 2) Test models: base fp16, int8 quant, 4-bit quant; 3) Toggle KV cache (on/off) and pre-warm vs cold; 4) Run under Dedicated vs Hosted. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 per-step.
[05:20] Maya Lopez: That sounds good. For the sample, we can provide 1 hour of traffic including burst scenarios. We'll also annotate calls that require database lookups so you can simulate KV miss patterns.
[05:29] Ruth Chen: Perfect. A few gotchas to call out: if you run in your VPC peered path, the NAT gateway and firewall stateful inspections can time out long-lived TCP streams that our streaming uses - that can cause chunk retransmits and high tails. For on-prem we'll recommend keeping streaming connections sticky to avoid re-negotiation.
[05:45] Priya Singh: Our infra team can add sticky sessions, though in some AZs we use autoscaling LBs which complicate stickiness.
[05:52] Samir Patel: Another lever is to pre-allocate connections from a connection pool on the app side so you don't pay the TCP handshake penalty at tail.
[05:59] Jon Kim: Regarding retries - our client library retries on 5xx after a backoff. Could that worsen p99?
[06:05] Ruth Chen: Yes, retries that occur without idempotency keys can cause duplicate work and queue congestion. Also, if the retry window is misaligned with batching windows you can cause thundering effects. We recommend idempotency and client-side jittered backoff tuned to batch windows.
[06:18] Maya Lopez: Do you support partial-result caching for common prefixes?
[06:22] Ruth Chen: We do. Prefix-level KV caching + chunked caching - you can cache intermediate KV states so subsequent generations for the same prefix skip the first N layers. That reduces both median and tail for conversational workloads.
[06:33] Jon Kim: Can you quantify the expected p99 reduction with a good cache hit pattern?
[06:36] Ruth Chen: It's very workload dependent. In a case study we saw p99 drop from ~1.8s to ~350ms for that flow when hit rate went from 20% to 80% and kernel path stayed consistent. But if network hops add 300ms, the benefit is smaller unless you also remove that network jitter.
[06:52] Priya Singh: We also noted disk I/O when the model was swapped in under memory pressure. Does Redwood handle cold-start model swap in a way that affects tail?
[06:59] Ruth Chen: Model swap can add seconds if weights are on remote storage. In Dedicated we keep active model sets resident; for hosted with many models we use a working set and you'll see occasional cold swaps. For critical endpoints we recommend pinning model versions on Dedicated or pre-loading in Private.
[07:14] Samir Patel: Quick interruption - Maya, what's your SLA target for p99?
[07:18] Maya Lopez: Ideally under 600ms for our chat endpoint p99, and under 2s for the batch reporting flow.
[07:24] Samir Patel: Good, that's actionable. We'll map recommendations to those targets.
[07:27] Ruth Chen: On batching knobs: adjust max batch size, max wait (ms), and slot time. For low-latency flows set max wait to 8-12ms and smaller max batch sizes; for throughput set larger waits. Also monitor queue depth histograms - long tails usually coincide with queue depth spikes.
[07:45] Jon Kim: How about kernel selection - does your runtime choose different kernels for different seq lengths? We have sequences from 32 to 2048 tokens.
[07:52] Ruth Chen: Yes kernel selection is sequence-length-aware. Some optimized matmul kernels are only valid up to a certain sequence length; beyond that we fall back to a slower but correct kernel. If your workload mixes short and very long sequences, those long-seq requests will dominate p99. One mitigation is sequence bucketing: route long-seq requests to a dedicated worker pool.
[08:10] Maya Lopez: Sequence bucketing - would that be a manual rule or can Redwood auto-route?
[08:14] Samir Patel: We support policy-based routing. You can define rules by sequence length, model, or route, and route to pools tuned for long sequences (larger memory, different kernel choices).
[08:24] Priya Singh: On VPC connectivity, is there support for private link or cross-account peering? Our compliance folks prefer PrivateLink/IAM-based peering.
[08:31] Ruth Chen: We support VPC peering and PrivateLink options for Private deployments. For Hosted, customers usually use a secure tunnel but PrivateLink gives best latency+security profile. We'll include options in the documentation pack.
[08:43] Jon Kim: Any experience with p99 behavior over multi-region failover? We plan to route to another region on failover.
[08:50] Ruth Chen: Multi-region failover adds DNS propagation and cold-cache effects. You'll likely see increased p99 immediately after failover due to cold caches and different kernel optimizations per region. Our recommended pattern: warm the secondary with a shadow traffic replay and a cold-cache pre-warm before cut-over.
[09:06] Maya Lopez: About observability - what dashboards should we look at specifically for tail?
[09:11] Ruth Chen: Key metrics: request ingress latency, queue wait time, model exec time, kernel execution histograms, KV cache hit/miss rates, network hop latency per hop, and streaming chunk timing. We'll provide a dashboard template.
[09:22] Samir Patel: We'll also attach an example query to compute p99 contribution by component - e.g., p99_total - p99_exec - p99_network = p99_other, to find where tail sits.
[09:32] Jon Kim: For the benchmark, can we test with our client-side retry policy and without, to measure amplification?
[09:37] Ruth Chen: Yes we'll run both. We'll also instrument idempotency keys to avoid duplicate work on retries.
[09:42] Maya Lopez: Any more mitigation options on the software side?
[09:45] Ruth Chen: Timeouts tuned to batch windows, client-side pooling, jittered backoff, sequence bucketing, pre-warming, prefix caching, and routing long sequences to dedicated pools. Also quantify how quantization changes CPU/GPU utilization to predict queue spikes.
[09:59] Priya Singh: Are there specific kernel versions or CUDA drivers that are known to cause jitter?
[10:03] Ruth Chen: Occasionally older drivers can regress for certain matmul paths. We'll include recommended driver/kernel versions for the tested stack; part of the benchmark will capture that.
[10:11] Samir Patel: Let's surface a tentative timeline: Ruth runs baseline benchmarks this week using Quasar sample trace; we deliver initial p95/p99 breakdown by 2026-10-12; then we do a follow-up deep dive to decide Dedicated vs Private pilot.
[10:25] Maya Lopez: Sounds good.
[10:27] Jon Kim: Quick question - how do you measure p99 across streaming? Do you take time-to-first-byte or time-to-final-token?
[10:33] Ruth Chen: We measure both. For streaming UX use time-to-first-byte (TTFB) p99; for correctness and billing present time-to-final-token p99. We'll report both so you can align SLOs.
[10:45] Maya Lopez: One oddity we saw: TTFB p99 was good, but final-token p99 terrible for some requests. That suggests server-side stalls mid-generation. What could cause that?
[10:54] Ruth Chen: Mid-generation stalls often relate to KV cache retrieval mid-seq (rare) or I/O when hitting some fallback logic, or garbage collection on host for orchestrator metadata. Kernel preemption from other high-priority tasks can also cause that.
[11:07] Samir Patel: We'll look at host-level OS metrics for those timestamps in the traces.
[11:11] Priya Singh: We'll share our NAT gateway logs and load balancer histograms.
[11:15] Ruth Chen: Great. A few more notes - for on-prem we recommend colocating the KV store with the inference workers, use huge pages for memory allocation to reduce TLB misses, and prefer RDMA between hosts if available to reduce host-host transfer latency for KV.
[11:31] Jon Kim: RDMA is on our wishlist but difficult to justify across all racks.
[11:35] Ruth Chen: Even enabling RDMA for heavy KV lanes can materially cut p99 in multi-GPU shards. We'll include a cost/benefit note.
[11:42] Maya Lopez: Anything else about batching when mixing streaming and non-streaming workloads on same pool?
[11:49] Ruth Chen: Mixing workloads is tricky - streaming often prefers small batches and low latency, while the bulk flows prefer large batches. We recommend separate worker pools or dynamic autoscaling that can shift pools between priorities. Redwood's routing layer can enforce per-route pool assignment.
[12:04] Jon Kim: For our pilot, we'd like to test three configs: Hosted default, Hosted Dedicated, and Private VPC with pre-warmed models. Can you estimate time to set those up?
[12:12] Samir Patel: Hosted default is immediate for benchmarks. Dedicated provisioning we can spin up a reserved pool in 2-3 days once capacity is allocated. Private VPC depends on network approvals but typical setup time is 1-2 weeks. We'll help accelerate.
[12:24] Ruth Chen: For the benchmark design I'll propose: step 1 baseline (no cache), step 2 warm cache, step 3 mixed traffic with spikes, step 4 long-seq bucketed test, and step 5 streaming chunk tuning. We'll capture kernel traces at millisecond granularity.
[12:39] Maya Lopez: Ok. One more practical - can you produce a CSV with every p99 outlier timestamp and the component-level breakdown? That will help root cause.
[12:47] Ruth Chen: Yes we can, we'll produce a p99 outlier table with component columns.
[12:51] Samir Patel: Any regulatory constraints we need to be aware of for traces?
[12:55] Priya Singh: We can't share user PII; traces must be sanitized. Also audit logs must be retained on-prem per our policy.
[13:03] Ruth Chen: Noted. We'll produce sanitized traces and a recommended retention policy map.
[13:08] Maya Lopez: Great. If there's no other immediate questions, let's recap next steps.
[13:12] Samir Patel: Recap: Ruth runs bench and shares results by 2026-10-12; Samir sends SOC2 + Dedicated pricing + VPC onboarding docs by 2026-10-06; Quasar shares sample trace and infra diagrams by 2026-10-08. We'll schedule follow-up pilot planning call for the week of 2026-10-12.
[13:29] Jon Kim: Confirmed.
[13:31] Maya Lopez: Thanks everyone.
[13:33] Ruth Chen: Thanks, bye.
[13:35] Samir Patel: Bye.

(Transcription notes: occasional filler words and interruptions preserved; some product names transcribed as generic terms e.g., "KV cahce" in one spot; timestamps approximate every 10-90 seconds per segment.)
